fields.title: Smena: Five Research Requests and Two People
fields.summary: Every department brought its own question. Decide what you will research.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you research this quarter and how?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Smena, responsible for research.
fields.brief/company: Smena is a fictional shift scheduling service for small cafes and stores. 3,400 paying locations.
fields.brief/context: Five research requests arrived for the quarter. There are two researchers, already half-booked. Simultaneously, management wants metrics cleaned up: every team has its own dashboard and numbers conflict.
fields.brief/constraints: Two researchers working half-time for one quarter. You can pick at most two requests.
fields.brief/task: Choose what to research, how, and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Research Without a Decision Is Just a Report
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The first test for any request is: what will we do differently depending on the answer? If there is no answer, skip the research—this frees capacity for areas with high cost of error. The second filter is method: stated intent measured by surveys is worth nothing, while half of questions can be answered by breaking down existing data.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
1. Marketing: 'study user satisfaction'. When asked what decision depends on results, they reply: 'we'll understand where we stand'.

2. Sales: 'find out if clients are willing to pay for a time tracking module'. Decision: whether to build the module (est. 4 months dev).

3. Support: 'understand why single-location cafes churn at month three'. Decision: whether to introduce a simplified tier (est. 1 quarter dev).

4. Founder: 'see what competitors are doing'. No decision specified.

5. Design: 'check if the new schedule publishing screen is clear'. Screen releases in three weeks; redesign takes one week.

Last year's 40-page report 'Persona of a Smena User' was opened 11 times all year.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Annual churn by location count: single location—31%, 2–3 locations—12%, more than 3—7%.

Among churned single-location accounts, 68% published zero schedules in their final month.

Last quarter a survey asked about willingness to pay for the time tracking module: 71% replied 'yes, interested'. The module wasn't built then.

Product analytics show: single-location accounts average 4 employees and publish schedules biweekly rather than weekly.

Support frequently hears from them: 'paper is easier for us, we only have four people'.

Usability testing on the schedule publishing screen has never been conducted.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
28 metrics are presented at all-hands meetings. No primary metric is assigned.

The growth team tracks signups and activations; product tracks published schedules; support tracks ticket volume.

Published schedules grew 19% this quarter. Annualized churn rose from 14% to 17% in the same period—never once discussed in meetings.

The same term 'active' means three different things in three reports: logged in within 30 days, published a schedule, or paying.

Location-count breakdowns don't exist in general reports—they live only in custom analyst exports upon request.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Two researchers, each available half of the time: the rest of the time goes to supporting current launches.

Interviews with churned clients are hard to organize: about every fifth agrees, eight conversations take two weeks.

A usability test with 6 people takes 3 days including analysis.

A survey sent to the user base can be dispatched in a day, bringing in about 400 responses.

The founder asked about competitors twice in a month and, judging by the conversation, expects an overview rather than a decision.

Cost of error: time tracking module — 4 months of team effort; simplified plan — a quarter; publication screen — a week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Take two decision-linked requests and fix metrics
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Filter out requests lacking clear decisions, select single-location churn and publishing screen usability, while establishing a primary metric with guardrails in parallel.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Filtering takes two meetings. Satisfaction and competitor overview are dropped: neither is tied to a decision; for the founder, you produce a half-day summary instead of a full study.
Single-location churn is taken first: cost of error is one quarter, and existing data hints at the answer—68% of churned users published no schedules, and support notes 'paper is easier'. Eight interviews over two weeks confirm: with 4 employees, scheduling takes 5 minutes on paper, and a cheaper tier won't change that. A quarter of dev work is saved.
Usability testing on the new screen takes three days, uncovers two issues, and fixes them a week before launch.
Time tracking isn't researched via surveys: past 71% 'interest' was worthless. Instead, sales is tasked with getting pre-payments from three clients.
Metrics are structured into a hierarchy: primary—share of locations publishing schedules on time; guardrails—churn and support tickets. A 19% rise in published schedules alongside rising churn stops looking like a success.
Trade-off: marketing and the founder didn't get dedicated studies, requiring clear explanations.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Saying no harms relationships. Conduct a mini-study for each request: satisfaction survey, time tracking survey, a few interviews, competitor overview, quick screen test.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The quarter ends with five reports. None lead to a decision.
The satisfaction survey produces a score with nothing to compare against.
The time tracking survey repeats last year's result: 74% answer 'interested'.
Interview count for churned clients drops to four instead of eight; findings are tentative and unused.
The usability test happens post-launch due to lack of time.
The founder reads the competitor overview and is satisfied.
Trade-off: everyone is temporarily happy, no decisions were altered, and next quarter starts with the same five requests.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Focus on the time tracking module
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: This is the most expensive decision—4 team months. Run a major study on willingness to pay: base survey and twenty interviews.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The cost of error was identified correctly—this is indeed the costliest decision of the quarter.
However, the method is wrong: survey yields 74% 'interested', interviews yield polite 'yes, would be useful'. Stated intent was measured instead of actual behavior; six months later the module launches and only 6% buy it.
No one checked last year's identical survey sitting in the archive.
The quarter was consumed by a single request, single-location churn went unaddressed, and screen usability went untested.
Trade-off: risk prioritization was correct, but validation methodology failed—willingness to pay is proven by pre-orders, not questions.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Until numbers align, any research will hang in the air. Spend a quarter on the metrics framework: unified definitions, hierarchy, breakdowns.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The work is essential and executed well: a primary metric, guardrails, unified definition of 'active', and location-count breakdowns appear in executive dashboards.
What was hidden becomes immediately visible: 19% schedule growth occurred alongside churn rising from 14% to 17%, with churn concentrated in single-location accounts.
However, the quarter ends there. The publishing screen launches untested, leaving users to uncover two bugs.
The single-location churn request remains open, despite the metric system pointing directly at it.
Trade-off: you built a tool you didn't have time to use, while three days for usability testing could always have been carved out.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Research isn't tied to a decision or concrete choices
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Metrics form a flat list without primary, driver, and guardrail roles
